Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function.

We've established recently, much like our work on de Sitter spacetime, that Fock's coordinate transformation doesn't constitute a canonical quantization method in Minkowski spacetime. This discovery led us to an intriguing finding - by applying his transformation, de Sitter spacetime can be viewed as a slowed-down version of Minkowski spacetime. In this paper, we'll demonstrate that using his transformation to re-examine the Minkowski vacuum state results in a shifted, zero-momentum mode. We represent this mode using a new set of creation and annihilation operators which are derived from the original ones. These new operators can be utilized to compute the energy-momentum correlation function of the Minkowski vacuum state. Furthermore, we derive the correlation function in de Sitter spacetime by incorporating a time-dilation factor, which is in line with the principles of special relativity.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework procures a top-three position in the Wikipedia Redirection Prediction track at the WSDM 2015 Challenge.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available.

Implicit copulas are an alternative to traditional copulas, designed to skip their separation into individual survival functions. This distinct feature allows them to bypass the limitation of 1-dimensional copula calculations, thereby expanding their applicability to negative data. This statistical approach has received considerable interest in recent years, as evidenced by the numerous conferences and workshops held on this topic. Our work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of implicit copulas for the broader mathematical community, building on previous work done by others.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the word2vec model, highlighting its reliance on Markovian assumptions that are tested and validated using real-world data. The paper also explores the implicit assumptions of a recent score-based method and assesses the implicit structures of pre-trained embeddings using a variety of tests. Our results suggest that the predictions of the word2vec model are consistent with the Markovian assumption but fail to capture the non-Markovian information present in the data, implying that word2vec-based embeddings may not fully capture the underlying structure of the language. Interestingly, our findings indicate that the score-based method is more effective in capturing the non-Markovian information, suggesting its potential as a more robust alternative to traditional word embedding models.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
A dynamic fixed-point algorithm is developed to solve the fair-throughput optimisation problem.
We also investigate the MISO-OFDM counterpart and show that the sum-throughput optimisation problem can be reformulated into a convex optimisation problem, solving which yields the optimal solution.
A dynamic fixed-point algorithm and successive convex approximation algorithm are proposed to solve the sum-throughput optimisation problem, with the former providing a faster convergence rate.
Numerical results are provided to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithms and compare them to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's vectorial representation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for each sentence through their tensoring of spin density matrices. This approach is demonstrated on a simple example using the benefits of controlled structural rules within a quantum interpretation. Furthermore, our proposal bridges the gap between linguistic type systems and the physical inspirations that drive them, showcasing that the control aspect of structural rules can be achieved without resorting to ad-hoc measures.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples to determine rationalizable equilibria when there are multiple coexisting rationalizable actions. Furthermore, even if the underlying model is perfectly known, the existing algorithm still requires an excessively large number of samples to determine rationalizable equilibria when there are an increasing number of players. Therefore, we tackle this challenge by introducing an efficient and player-agnostic algorithm that learns rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer games, and we establish a significantly more favorable sample complexity guarantee that is on the order of polynomial samples when the number of players is large. We also provide a theoretical analysis to compare our algorithm to the previous state-of-the-art method through an explicit numerical example, and the obtained results indicate that our algorithm outperforms the competing algorithm in every scenario we examined.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{R} \times (S^2_{-1}),$ with the Reeb vector field being a factor.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, a variation of the REINFORCE algorithm has been proposed. The new method, Variance Reduction based Experience Replay (VRER), is designed to enhance the effectiveness of policy updates. By dividing the optimization process into two stages – global optimization and a localized refinement – VRER is able to minimize the negative impact of noise on the policy updates. To overcome the limited sample size issue in each optimization stage, experience replay is employed to supplement the data used for policy updates. The proposed algorithm is efficient, easy to implement, and is expected to yield superior performance when compared to the standard REINFORCE algorithm, despite requiring significantly fewer samples for each policy update.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes it easy to work with polynomial operators used in the quantum many-body theory by creating a specialized language for their manipulation. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive toolkit for the development of exact diagonalization codes, carefully designed for high performance, ease of use, and customization. libcommute boasts an intuitive syntax for commonly applied abstractions and algorithms, and its extensive documentation and comprehensive unit tests guarantee its stability. Furthermore, the Python 3 wrapper called pycommute provides a useful solution for smaller-scale diagonalization problems, quick prototyping, and the seamless integration of libcommute's performance-driven computational cores with Python applications.

Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. We employed high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ to resolve this controversy. Our results show the band back-bending due to strong correlation on the dose, and by calculating the band structure near the Fermi surface with inclusion of strong correlation and band shifting, we were able to determine the true band structure and remove artificial superconducting gap structures. As a result, we found that the superconducting gap is $0.8\sim1.0$ times the electronic Fermi velocity on the EFC, consistent with $s$-wave symmetry.

Two new versions of the supersymmetric bosonization formula have been derived, which can be compared to the traditional method of using the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. While both approaches yield equivalent results, they have distinct advantages and may be more useful in specific contexts. The new formulas are more complex than the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, but they provide more explicit relationships between supersymmetric fields and can be viewed as more natural extensions of the bosonization formula. Furthermore, one of the new formulas has the same variance as the Dirac fermion as the bosonized field, which may be preferable when the fermion zero-mode plays a significant role.

Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

Our research is centered on enhancing the maximum achievable capacity in a wireless communication system, comprising multiple input and output antennas and a surface capable of intelligent signal reflection. To provide an accurate assessment, we take into consideration the impact of correlated signal weakening and a phenomenon in which the intensity and phase of the reflected signal are interconnected, often disregarded in theoretical studies. By employing a mathematical approach that accounts for large-scale trends and phase shifts, we are able to formulate a detailed description of the system's performance and determine the maximum achievable capacity in terms of these factors. Moreover, our approach enables efficient management of system parameters to achieve optimal performance, reducing the need for continuous system recalibration and assessment. Monte Carlo simulations validate our analytical findings, revealing how different system design parameters influence performance, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in optimizing performance in scenarios with correlated signal weakening.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular design enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings in the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the results from LES and DNS on reaction rate amplitude and phase shift.

We've discovered a hidden characteristic of stars, which originates from a topological property, by drawing parallels between stellar behavior and that of topological insulators. To understand stellar oscillations, we created a mathematical framework that identifies the embedded phase space of stellar modes and established an equivalent to the Bianchi identity in stellar dynamics. This results in constraints on the formation of edge modes, which are complex oscillatory patterns that emerge when multiple modes intersect. The existence of these edge modes is equivalent to the stability of the stationary phases, which in turn affects the stability of the star itself. Furthermore, we found that in stars, these edge modes appear as nonlinear periodic motions, which could be observable with future missions equipped to detect tiny magnetic field variations induced by stellar seismic waves.

We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the speed at which chimera states propagate. To facilitate
understanding, we illustrate our method through a specific example involving a ring
network of phase oscillators with type II neurons. However, we emphasize that this method
is broadly applicable across a wide range of non-locally coupled networks.

In certain two-dimensional spin models with significant site-to-site interactions, like the extended-Hubbard and XXZ models, robust, self-organizing clusters are observed at adjacent sites. These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple time scales and a mixed Poisson distribution in the long-term correlation between separated sites. Specifically, in a larger distance, the correlation decays according to a power law, with an exponent that reflects the number of available cluster paths between those sites.

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number. By taking into consideration the effects of e-foldings in the early universe and the influence of a non-zero efficiency at the present time, we formulate a comprehensive estimate of the effect on the $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay lifetime. When the dark matter mass lies beneath $10^{-22}$eV, the influence on the $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay lifetime surpasses the Heidelberg-Moscow limit by several orders of magnitude. Conversely, the impact on the cosmological density of neutrinos remains insignificant.

The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons and limitations of existing methods in identifying them prompt research on new approaches to simulation and observational strategies. One such approach, presented in this report, involves novel indicators to indirectly identify these photons by observing cosmic ray phenomena composed of spatially correlated air showers of multiple cosmic rays observed simultaneously. The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between the solar magnetic field and the incoming photons, using the GAMES3R and M5D/M5D-Solene codes, to predict the predicted distribution of cosmic rays and resulting phenomena in the atmosphere. The expected distribution of cosmic rays with high energies and low multiplicities, as well as the expected distribution of multiplicity across all energies, are used as indicators of the hypothetical photons' existence. The proposed method also includes strategies for validating the indirect signs of photons against theoretical predictions through comparisons of the predicted and actual distributions of cosmic rays with respect to their arrival directions and feeding patterns of certain riometric systems. If verified, the methods presented here can be applied to search for photons across a broader spectral range and in studies of cosmic rays across all energies.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be confirmed through data from gravitational redshift and lensing effects.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access despite failures demands the use of concurrent updates across replicated data. A specific approach to this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Although various CRDT designs have been proposed in the past, there is a lack of unifying theory to explain their underlying principles and facilitate their development. This paper introduces a design framework called Remove-Win that provides a comprehensive theory of CRDTs, making it possible for programmers to design their own CRDTs using this framework. To illustrate its effectiveness, we present two new CRDT designs developed using the Remove-Win framework, a Set CRDT and a Counter CRDT, in addition to their implementations in Haskell and Python. This framework can be employed in courses on concurrent systems programming to guide students in designing their own CRDTs. The Python implementation of Remove-Win is also suitable for assignments and lab exercises.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of a surveyed sample of low-mass neutron star binaries in the Milky Way exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the All-Sky Monitor on the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada Telescope. Also, it was found that the observed short recurrence times are not representative of the entire population of such binaries. Consequently, we determine the likelihood that the Galactic Center quiescent X-ray binaries include neutron star binaries with long recurrence times to be greater than 75%.

The velocity distribution pattern of distant binary star systems can be an effective means of determining how gravity behaves at low acceleration rates, typically found on the outskirts of galaxies. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane orthogonal to their collective movement across the sky. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from large angles, simulations indicate a relatively low uncertainty of around 30 meters per second in velocity measurements when line velocities are taken into account, rather than projected sky velocities with an uncertainty of around 100 meters per second.

However, due to the smaller uncertainty in line velocities, a much larger sample of wide binary star systems would be required to distinguish the Newtonian gravitational model from Modified Newtonian Dynamics models. Nonetheless, the paper suggests potential avenues for further research, such as utilizing the velocity distribution of distant binary star systems in the direction of the galactic center, which could provide more stringent constraints between these two models with a significantly smaller required sample size of wide binary star systems.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

We analyze the impact of acoustic waves on one-dimensional flows in general,
focusing particularly on massive stars experiencing outbursts exceeding the
Eddington limit. By leveraging approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the
classical equal-area technique to include both integral and differential forms.
We model and simulate shock behavior within initially finite sinusoidal wave
trains, identifying distinct patterns for internal shocks, and both head and tail
shocks, and confirming that our predictions align with numerical simulations.
The findings reveal that our new expressions for shock heating rates provide a
more accurate account of the internal shock dynamics. We also predict that
shocks from head and tail waves will interact in $t\approx 2M^{-1/s}t_{\rm dyn}$
and result in the formation of a nonlinear wave with $5/3$ power law and
critical density $\rho_c=\rho_0(1.77)^{1/s}$, while the wave's leading edge
will behave as a nascent blastwave with a constant energy release and
self-similar velocity $v\propto t^{-1/s}$ for $t\gg t_{\rm dyn}$.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity of multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight, though 
the former must be significantly greater than the latter in quantity.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten and has since become a major area of study in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras. These notes have a dual purpose: to provide an approachable introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with basic representation theory knowledge and to address a noticeable lack in the existing literature by bringing together key results from the field in a comprehensive overview.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity.

Automated driving systems depend on predictive modules to assess risks and avoid accidents, however, their current implementation is hindered by expensive and complex technologies. A novel artificial intelligence approach has been developed for classifying high-risk maneuvers from a single camera, using pre-trained image processing algorithms to improve performance and efficiency. This advanced system utilizes deep learning and temporal sequence analysis to recognize patterns of behavior from a dataset with annotated risk indicators, and was optimized using various feature extractors for maximum effectiveness, ultimately achieving a 0.937 AUC score.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions by incorporating the effects of rotation on structure and evolution, considering both equilibrium and non-equilibrium mixings in the presence of hydrogen burning. The simulations demonstrate that rotation can significantly expand the range of stable, low-mass stars, increasing the upper limit of the Chandrasekhar mass ratio by up to $\eta_\textrm{SHB}/0.4\approx1.4$ for spinning objects, shedding mass and heat, and potentially resulting in binary black hole formation.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
artificial neural networks. Although widely adopted in other contexts, these methods 
have not been heavily employed for amplitude analyses. The article also introduces 
new applications for these models, such as leveraging sidebands to determine the 
density of background in multiple dimensions, as well as more comprehensive density 
estimation utilizing artificial neural networks.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that when a kick or other disturbance occurs during locomotion, our feedback system helps the robot recover from the setback, even when there is significant loss of balance and footing.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ on the field of rational functions $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$ has a simple, almost arithmetic nature. Specifically, for any nonzero element $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_q(t)$, the value $\text{val}(\alpha)$ always lies on the edge of the lattice formed by the values of the elements of the finite field $k$. This phenomenon does not hold for infinite fields $K$. For example, the total residue map on $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(t)$ contains values like $\sqrt{2}$ in its domain. In an attempt to generalize this arithmetic property of residue fields, we show that if a field $K$ is equipped with an extension of the total residue map, then its value group must be isomorphic to a direct sum of copies of the real numbers and the integers. As a result, we also demonstrate that for any nonzero element $\alpha \in K$, the value $\text{val}(\alpha)$ always lies on the edge of a lattice formed by the values of the elements of a subfield of $K$. This implies that if a field $K$ is equipped with an order-preserving map $\text{val}$, then its value group is isomorphic to a direct sum of copies of the real numbers and the integers.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates two novel attack strategies.  Firstly, it combines two previously identified attack channels to achieve a more significant overall effect.  Secondly, it employs a new technique that uses a specially designed binary balloting mechanism.  A comprehensive evaluation of HyperDegrade was conducted on seven distinct CPU models, involving over 2000 side-channel measurements.  The analysis indicates that side-channel losses can be as low as 1.57%, and that HyperDegrade is highly robust, with an average success rate of 94.5% in 1000 trials, despite experiencing side-channel losses.  In realistic scenarios, HyperDegrade was found to be consistently effective, with an average frequency reduction of over two orders of magnitude in effective frequencies.  The evaluation also revealed that HyperDegrade can be as much as 24 times more accurate than previous degrading attacks, and that the side-channel data loss can be as high as 99.43%.  The study demonstrates that HyperDegrade can be as much as 24 times more accurate than previous degrading attacks, and that the side-channel data loss can be as high as 99.43%.  The study provides concrete evidence that frequent and gradual degrading can be as much as 24 times more accurate than one-time extreme degrading, and that the side-channel data loss can be as high as 99.

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

A precise LHCb method for determining the CKM angle gamma from decays at the tree level is explained. LHCb can generate up to 16 separate measurements, using different decay modes of various beauty and charm mesons, but they do not have the same level of sensitivity to gamma. By combining all available results, a highly accurate value can be obtained. These proceedings provide a detailed overview of several independent determinations used for this combined result and report the most recent outcome available as of Summer 2018.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant with a third order. This innovation builds on a concept initially explored by the second author in his paper titled "A Vassiliev Invariant of Order Two from an Integrated 1-cocycle".

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider sterile neutrinos, establishing a minimum mass for a single such neutrino flavour of around 1.0 eV/c^2.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity.

In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model without exchanging sensitive information. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants collaborating on the same data attributes, whereas the latter involves collaboration on distinct data attributes among different individuals. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here, we concentrate on FL in the vertical mode and investigate various attacks on private data, revealing that certain attacks can successfully compromise the privacy of individual data sets even when the scale of training is modest, without needing to access the entire FL dataset. Additionally, our study reveals that certain attacks can successfully breach the L2-DP (layer 2-differential privacy) privacy of individual data sets, without needing to access the entire FL dataset, even when the scale of training is modest.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle of radius $1/\sqrt{n-2}$ and a circle of radius $1/\sqrt{n-2} - 1$.

Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they are trained with publicly available, labeled data sets (specifically, the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) set) and then tested against CMR data sets of TOF patients. We then compared these results to two alternative approaches: a smaller amount of training on a data set with more comprehensive information regarding heart abnormalities, and training on a larger data set of diverse cardiac conditions with only partial labeling. 

Our findings showed that even when trained and tested against a single type of cardiac condition (i.e., TOF vs. non-TOF), models that are trained on a diverse range of cardiac conditions using a larger data set with more comprehensive labeling achieve higher scores than those that are trained on a smaller data set with specific information

This study explores the long-term properties of phase-field functionals that incorporate slight variations within both their bulk and surface components. The considered functionals embody a specific type of static model that quantifies damage in heterogeneous materials. The model's ultimate behavior is comprehensively defined by Gamma-convergence based on the relative rates at which its approximations and oscillation parameters converge.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a splitter, allocates part of the frequency spectrum for information transmission and the remaining for energy capture. To analyze performance improvements, an optimization problem was created that maximizes energy gain and maintains a minimum data rate in a multi-user OFDMA network. Next, the model was refined to investigate throughput optimization in an SWIPT-enabled OFDMA system, resulting in a complex MINLP problem. Finally, an innovative harvesting technique based on a co-located receiver architecture and Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) was explored to improve the energy efficiency of wireless networks.

Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

Complex, multi-dimensional data is often analyzed with conditionally specified models, which rely on implicit assumptions at their boundaries. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. The method is then demonstrated with a widely used model, and an alternative condition is also introduced to address limitations in the original Heffernan-Tawn model, particularly regarding its inability to capture certain cases of asymptotic independence.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where the same word can have different meanings based on the context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build upon and improve previous work, particularly Huang et al's. GlossBERT model, which addresses WSD (Huang et al.,2019), we plan to enhance their results through modifications to their dataset, ensemble techniques, and replacing BERT with alternative transformer architectures like BART and ALBERT. A corresponding GitHub repository contains our code, which expands upon the original implementation provided by Huang et al.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. We discover that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, the presence of these planetary bodies is not necessarily confirmed. In this study, we explore the potential for vertically extended shear instabilities to explain the formation of certain structural patterns in disks surrounding young stars. Our model involves the gravitational connection of multiple ring structures in disks and predicts how their formation might be shaped by key factors, including the amplitude of density variations and the radius at which they occur. By applying this model to a range of situations, we attempt to match its predictions with observational data. The results indicate that in certain cases, structures formed through shear instabilities can be distinguished using high-resolution observations. Furthermore, our study suggests that in some systems, features resembling spiral arms and localized curved formations may develop without the presence of detectable planetary bodies, which could instead be the result of shear instabilities triggered by ring structures in the disk.

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. Results show that BigApple predictations for finite nuclei and density properties of neutron star matter are diverse across the four forces. Nevertheless, all BigApple forces successfully match GW190814's data for the canonical density of neutron star matter.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing Wannier functions in the model. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption can lead to inaccuracies. For instance, a more complex spectral structure is revealed when the model incorporates additional correlated orbitals, a phenomenon not seen in the simpler model. Utilizing the Fork Tensor Product State impurity solver allows us to resolve high-frequency differences and obtain more precise results. Our results indicate that using this solver for full 5-band DMFT calculations yields spectral structures consistent with experiments, showcasing the solver's ability to perform such complex calculations directly on the real-frequency axis.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions.

Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of more accurate, detailed models that capture the underlying structure of the material. From these, we identified the smallest models that are stable and consistent with experimental data; two of these models can also be applied to similar materials. These discoveries open up possibilities for using computational modeling to design more effective materials. Additionally, we've determined that certain characteristics in barium titanate, such as the movement of certain atoms and the vibration of the molecular structure, can be controlled through changes to the volume of the material, and further that these changes are influenced by the presence of certain other atoms.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound.

The unit interval data best fit the beta model; however, the standard beta distribution falls short when dealing with bimodal unit interval data. A novel, bimodal beta distribution is presented, based on an approach utilizing the alpha-skew-normal model. We examine key characteristics of this distribution, including bimodality, real moments, entropy measures, and its unique identifiability. A regression model is also proposed, based on this new distribution, along with a discussion of residual properties. Estimation is achieved via maximum likelihood, supported by a Monte Carlo simulation evaluating the efficacy of these estimators in finite samples, along with a discussion of the outcomes. A real-world application illustrates the proposed distribution's aptitude in modeling data sets with bimodal patterns.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit.

In a gyroscopic Sagnac interferometer, typically used for calibrating a gyroscope's angular momentum, a notable spectral shift around anomalies occurs. This spectral shift within the rotating gyroscope can be understood in relation to the longitudinal Doppler shift experienced by the opposing light beams in the Sagnac interferometer.

Considering an irreducible simple algebraic group $G$ and a Borel subgroup $B$, let's analyze a subgroup $P$ that contains $B$. Further, let's derive the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $P$, denoted by $\mathfrak m$. According to Richardson's theorem, the algebra $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$ of $P$ semi-invariants is multiplicity-free. A key linear subvariety, known as a Weierstrass section, exists where the action of $P'$ on $\mathfrak m$ induces an isomorphism onto the subvariety. A specific Weierstrass section is constructed in type $A$ with improved form and a focus shifted from its construction to its application. Given the action of the group, a set of points $\mathscr N$ can be determined. From this construction, a point $e$ in $\mathscr N$ can be derived. A particular $B$ saturation set can be used to provide an explicit description of a component $\mathscr C$ in $\mathscr N$. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end, self-alignment strategy that separates face pose from alignment, using a pose code derived from a face manifold to guide the reconstruction process. To enhance robustness, we incorporate multiple strategies, including the use of a mask code for occlusion correction, noise modeling, and learning, as well as introducing misaligned data to help the network learn from distortions. Exhaustive experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach in compared methods, yielding superior performance on benchmark datasets and spurring the introduction of the AdaptoCon code to address adaptation challenges.

We investigate the concurrent loss of spatial translation and dilation symmetries in a class of models inspired by the Ginzburg-Landau theory, in which the mechanisms responsible for symmetry breaking are represented by a potential function describing spatial gradients. Our research reveals the existence of modes with subdimensional or zero propagation, characterized as "fractons", where their motion is constrained. The effective field theories of this type encompass systems like helical superfluids and metafluids, in which fractons can be linked to an underlying symmetry associated with higher order charges, resulting in the simplification of some elastic properties. Introducing a finite charge density influences the fracton's mobility, leading to a trade-off between the chemical potential and superfluid velocity in determining the gap of the dilaton. The mobility of fractons can also be modified at zero charge by introducing a long-range interaction between the superfluid's condensate and the collective mode of the superfluid.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. These predictions align with forecasts from LISA and other gravitational wave detectors, with a significant overlap in the $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ estimates.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data.
