We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness.
This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as high-risk consumers or not. Among the tested options, a top-performing model using decision trees showed particular promise, with an accuracy of 89.4 percent in predicting high-risk consumption. The model's performance was also examined across different datasets, including those with combined data from multiple sources. The findings indicated that even with combined data, the accuracy can reach as high as 85.7 percent. A key aspect of this research involved assessing the reliability of personality assessments, taking into consideration the risk of false positives and false negatives. Ultimately, it was concluded that the most skilled models can achieve a high degree of accuracy, with a margin of error of less than 11 percent, in predicting high-risk consumption patterns.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, actual HHL executions on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum machines are impeded by gate errors, readout uncertainties, and non-ideal classical regression techniques. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, a hybrid approach that modifies HHL to accommodate the peculiarities of these machines and enhances its performance. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of this method by optimizing portfolios of up to 100 assets with real-world data, demonstrating that NISQ-HHL outperforms the classical method by a factor of twenty in computational time.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. Nonetheless, the optimal average cross-sectional volume cannot be achieved unless cross-sections pass through the centroid of the shape. Therefore, the focus is on stationary shapes with optimal average cross-section properties. A new formula is introduced for average cross-section calculations in any dimension, and the associated equation of stationary shapes is derived. Characteristics of stationary shapes are discussed through mathematical derivation, numerical modeling, and graphical visualization. Additionally, the distinct properties of stationary shapes in 2D, 3D, and 5D are explored and analyzed.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates, with a particularly high estimated mass that conflicts with equilibrium surface temperatures or a previously reported irregular rotation period, for which we hypothesize possible explanations, including a highly elliptical orbit, or the dwarf having a substantial irregular shape that could be the result of a gravitational interaction with its host star, validated through a thorough analysis, including the retrieval of physical parameters with a cutting-edge code, providing a more precise understanding of this famous T-dwarf.

Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. We demonstrate how lattice simulations can determine the minimum virtuality for a photon needed for Bjorken scaling to apply to structure functions. Additionally, we explain the parton model representation of the structure functions within the Bjorken limit and assess its coherence. In line with typical DIS on protons, a kinematic parameter $x$ here directly represents the momentum carried by the partons, with its value spanning from zero to infinity. If the partons' momenta are parametrized as $x T u$, with $u$ being the four-velocity of the fluid and $T$ the temperature in its rest frame, the distribution of quarks within the non-interacting quark plasma follows $x \log(1+e^{-x/T})$.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, is primarily a theoretical object in model simulations of particle physics. The quark composition of this particle makes up about 86% of its total mass. Due to its scarce occurrence in normal conditions, very little is known about the Ω-baryon's properties. Theoretical predictions indicate that in high-energy environments, this particle could decompose into different mesons in various ways, offering a potential route for its detection. Theoretical models also forecast that in its ground state, the Ω-baryon will not exhibit any significant electric dipole moment, which could be verified through precision measurements of its electromagnetic properties. Theoretical estimates of the Ω-baryon's decay width to a photon and a meson still vary greatly, which could be resolved by the spectroscopic study of this particle in different conditions. The study suggests that in hadronic matter under strain, the Ω-baryon may be detectable in a range of energies that could be accessed by next-generation experiments.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

Building on cutting-edge experimental projects such as HIBEF at the XFEL, our calculations investigate the birefringent scattering of x-rays when interacting with two combined optical lasers, considering various possible outcomes. To aid in detecting quantum vacuum effects experimentally, our analysis focuses particularly on situations where x-ray photons show differences not just in polarization, but also in direction of propagation and potential energy changes.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a specific form of encryption where an adversary is unable to produce more than one encryption of a given plaintext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a particular unclonable encryption scheme that allows for the secure transmission of unique messages of varying lengths. This scheme is based on post-quantum principles and enables the creation of multiple unclonable encryptions of distinct plaintexts. Furthermore, this scheme enables the verification of a receiver's knowledge of a specific encryption without revealing additional information about the receiver's clonable and unclonable encryptions.

  - Key Size Proportions: We've established a specific unclonable encryption scheme with a key size that is at least half as large as the plaintext it protects. This achievement is based on classical constructions and significantly reduces the necessary key size compared to other encryption methods.

  - Forward Security: We've also explored a particular unclonable encryption scheme that maintains security even after an adversary gains access to the receiver's storage. This scheme is based on post-quantum principles and ensures that an adversary is unable to produce more than one encryption of a given plaintext, even with unlimited storage and computational power.

This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message in its designated area. It was demonstrated
that modifying an existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission
with very low probability of error, yet this modification is identifiable to an
all-powerful adversary. Furthermore, increasing the bandwidth of transmission can
increase the security breach probability approaching 1. A modified version of an
existing communication protocol achieved very low error rates in authenticating
messages in certain scenarios.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. While Anomalous Hall effect was found to be sensitive to the Bismuth layer's thickness, an increase in this thickness led to a decrease in the Anomalous Hall effect, contradicting expectations for Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect. It is proposed that scattering at the Cobalt/Bismuth interface instead dominates the Anomalous Hall effect, while the Bismuth layer's resistance influences its magnitude. This finding is supported by a model that takes into account both the scattering at the interface and the Cobalt/Bismuth multilayer's resistance. As a result, the threshold resistance of the Bismuth layer needs to be considered in the search for Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in ferromagnetic multilayers.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with a global network of telescopes. Although the new data does not significantly alter the existing estimate of the planet's orbital path, it does improve the accuracy of that estimate. As a result, the schedule for JWST observations of HD80606b needs to be revised to take into account the updated orbital parameters, which could affect the alignment of the planet and its star during future transits.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is utilized to efficiently generate relevant events, and we utilize these calculations to predict key observables of the Drell-Yan process with high accuracy. Our analysis is relevant to the LHC's search for specific types of vector leptoquarks, which could exhibit lepton-flavour non-universality.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups (pregnant women, children) and re-scans for statistical improvement are unnecessary. Advanced machine learning models have been successful in estimating labelling masks for adaptive PET reconstructions. However, these models have limitations: they are typically optimized for in-distribution data and struggle with out-of-distribution data due to their non-robust design. Additionally, PET data is expensive to obtain, thus there's a need to explore sparse and uncertainty-aware labelisation strategies. This research introduces an uncertainty-aware neural network that learns optimal mask estimates while considering the physics behind PET measurements and the data's inherent noise. It uses a variational autoencoder and incorporates robustness to out-of-distribution data by adding a stable reconstruction path. Consequently, this model excels in cost-effective labelisation for lower-dose PET data without sacrificing accuracy.

The issue of tailoring news to individuals' interests while respecting their data remains unresolved. Growing worries about over-collected data and its unintended use have motivated our research on balancing personalization and privacy. Our experience creating personalized content platforms that protect users' confidentiality has sparked an investigation into users' attitudes towards these topics. A conducted survey revealed the opinions of various age groups regarding personalization and privacy. In this research, we are sharing our key discoveries with publishers and the community to inform the design and development of next-generation news recommender systems, which should prioritize the human user and achieve a harmonious balance between personalization and privacy.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer models that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer models can be inconsistent in their interpretation of the text, often making it difficult to determine if this inconsistency is a result of their ability to capture the coherence of the text or some other factor. Furthermore, the study finds that the computer models' tendency to make certain statements more important than others can be both consistent with the principles of CT and counter to those principles, depending on the context.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

The rising intricacy of modern adaptable systems demands elevated automation in their configuration process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated workflow integration. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved human understanding via metric-driven optimization. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to configuring a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets.

For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk around a black hole could supply $10^{22}\mathrm{W}$ of energy, sufficiently powering an estimated $10^{10}$ civilizations. However, to optimize energy usage, researchers propose leveraging the unique properties of an ENS in its own right, enabling a civilization to tap into $10^{50}\mathrm{quanta}$ of information carried by the environment. Furthermore, constructing a Sphere around a black hole may have the added benefit of preventing the civilization's own technological decline by limiting access to an ever-expanding information universe.

Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the identification of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering active measurement tools via P2P. We then outline a reference model for SLA breach detection, which includes components for active measurement, result collection, and alert generation. Furthermore, we describe possible implementations and outline future research directions for this concept.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barns, in line with existing theoretical models and exceeding the sensitivity of existing data by a factor of ten.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered that particles made of equal
parts water and silicate sticks most effectively when heated to approximately
300 Kelvin. A follow-up series of experiments was conducted to observe how
stickiness is affected by temperature increases from 300 Kelvin. The grains
were heated to different temperatures ranging from 300 Kelvin down to
protoplanetary disk conditions. In each case, a pair of grains with the same
composition was dropped into a 30 Kelvin water bath and their sticking
properties monitored. The results showed that even at elevated temperatures,
the optimal temperature for maximum stickiness remains at 300 Kelvin.
However, it's also evident that higher temperatures lead to a greater disparity
in how quickly the grains stick at different temperatures. A potential model
is presented to explain these findings, suggesting that heat causes the water
content to evaporate, resulting in a silicate-dominated surface and the loss
of sticking power. This model holds true for temperatures up to 500 Kelvin,
but above that, a different mechanism takes over and sticking is lost.
Consequently, we anticipate that particles with high water content will converge
at temperatures optimal for their composition, influencing how dust grows in
a protoplanetary disk.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness.

To extend the BFKL equation to include two gluons in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory, a key component is the one-loop amplitude of two gluons where one is emitted in a central role. This paper calculates this amplitude for all possible configurations of gluon polarizations. Although this amplitude is not directly obtainable through a simple extension of the BFKL equation due to a crossing symmetry, it can be derived from the amplitude of four gluons in a collinear configuration, sharing a small angle, through a symmetry transformation. In such a scenario, the four-gluon amplitude can be expressed through the impact factor and kernel functions, with the latter being related to the BFKL kernel. The calculation of the central-emission vertex is a crucial step in this transformation. The resulting expression allows for an interpretation of the BFKL equation as a component of a higher-loop equation, the KKLP equation, which describes the four-gluon amplitude in a collinear limit. This derivation holds for all possible configurations of gluon polarizations, as dictated by the N=4 SYM theory.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin-orbit coupling-induced magnetic moment, thus restoring long-range pair correlations. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling and Zeeman field may be simultaneously controlled to achieve topologically non-trivial phases of exact spin singlet superconductors.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, as a means of quantifying the effectiveness of action sequences produced by this method.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method and provides rate and distortion metrics for certain suboptimal detectors. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detectors such as the minimum mean square error detector and obtain closed-form distance metrics, which indicate that the 2-dimensional Euclidean distance is an relevant criterion. We also examine practical detectors such as the recursive least-squares method and propose a simplified approach that reduces computational demands. A simulation section compares the detection methods, including a novel approach, and considers system design parameters including the number of transmit and receive antennas, spatial modulation parameters, and the number of data streams.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
this updated catalog, we employed our visualization tools to model the spectral
energy distributions of 718 galaxies using a range of radiative processes and 10
imaging bands from various all-sky surveys. The catalog's sensitivity to the
spectral models and imaging observations was quantitatively assessed, and we've
made the catalog's underlying software framework openly available to the community
at voxastro.org.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction occurred over time within the South Atlantic basin.  Initial E-W to NE-SW rifting in the Juruaetaera rift of Brazil (located central in the basin) dated back to the Early Jurassic, with subsequent NE-SW focused extension beginning in the Middle to Late Jurassic.  This phase continued until the Early Cretaceous, with rift propagation towards the conjugate West African margin occurring in the Late Jurassic to Cretaceous periods.  Break-up in the central basin happened in the Early Cretaceous, whereas it occurred in the Aptian-Albian in the Brazilian and Congo Basins.  This delay in break-up time resulted in the neotectonic rift propagating towards the conjugate margin and interacting with pre-rift sediments in the Brazilian and Congo Basins until the Albian-Albian-Albian.  This re-examination of the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins offers a more detailed understanding of the complex and multi-directional extension occurring within the South Atlantic basin.

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the intricate configurations of knotted proteins using advanced topological methods. A novel statistical approach has been developed that utilizes Dirac's string field to describe the spatial arrangement of knotted proteins. The study introduces the concept of a closed Dirac string to identify whether a protein's native state is knotted. A more precise assessment of a protein's knotiness is made by analyzing the interaction of two closed Dirac strings. The proposed method is tested on a set of locally knotted proteins and the results are used to create a fold-by-fold comparison of their knotiness. The study finds that proteins with the same knot type have similar folding pathways, whereas those with distinct knot types have significantly different folding pathways. The data is also examined to identify any patterns that could indicate knot formation during protein folding. The research demonstrates that proteins with specific knot types follow distinct folding pathways compared to those that are not knotted, according to their secondary structure descriptions. However, when examining the distribution of knot formation across the protein sequence, no specific patterns were found that could indicate knot formation during protein folding.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear due to limitations of current constraints. By employing an independent methodology that utilizes a profile likelihood to analyze the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's optical reconstruction, we obtained a new estimation for the EDE density parameter. This approach yielded a value of $\Omega_{\rm EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ at 68% confidence, which when combined with other data sets, including the Baryon Acoustic Oscillations seen in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, resulted in an even more precise constraint of $\Omega_{\rm EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.029$.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing the NG theorem, we employed geometric and algebraic methods to clearly explain the theorem's mechanisms. A key aspect examined involves the laying down of flat directions in a Lagrangian, which is essentially a geometric representation of the F-flatness concept seen in algebraic geometry. The anomalous NG theorem has been demonstrated to emerge naturally from both the Schur lemma in Lie algebras and the geometric algebra's idempotent property. Our study also delves into the connections between the NG theorem and other theoretical concepts such as symmetry, as well as the role of symmetry in determining a vacuum state. Finally, we discuss the implications of the anomalous NG theorem on physical systems, using both the SU(3)$\times$SU(2)$\times$U(1) quark model and the Wess-Zumino model as examples.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate the effectiveness of counterfactual data generated by DISCO relative to a baseline crowd-sourced dataset, showcasing that it yields a more compact and precise dataset that significantly enhances the performance of models trained on it. Moreover, we find that models trained on DISCO-generated data possess superior generalization capabilities, particularly in settings with limited labeled data or across linguistic domains.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it adopts a unique balanced remote/van der Waals mixed epitaxial mode. The use of low-energy electron diffraction and scanning tunneling microscopy revealed GdPtSb films exhibit both misoriented grains and a pinhole structure, characteristic of a combination of remote and van der Waals growth. Notably, this balanced mode is susceptible to external factors such as annealing temperatures, leading to a shift towards either remote or van der Waals epitaxy. The possibility of obtaining the balanced mode might depend on specific heating methods. Consequently, it is advisable to use slow thermal processing. The evaluation of the magnetic and electrical properties of these films showed they retain their Heusler compound characteristics despite the growth on free standing graphene, which is susceptible to strain from the substrate. The findings of this study indicate that the choice of annealing temperature can influence the graphene surface, thereby allowing for the achievement of the balanced remote/van der Waals epitaxial mode.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero and as time approaches infinity. The upper bound can be perceived as a nonlocal-in-time modified energy, which includes both the original energy and a cumulative component stemming from the memory effect of the time-fractional derivative. Specifically, it demonstrates that the original energy actually declines as time passes in a localized area near the starting point. Although the theory mainly focuses on the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, it can be applied to other time-fractional phase-field models like the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

In discrete time, first-order L1 and second-order L2 schemes for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation exhibit analogous decreasing modified energies, facilitating the verification of stability. Several numerical experiments have been conducted to display the behavior of the modified energy and confirm our theoretical findings.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be understood within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique also facilitates easy integration into handheld devices used for cardiac auscultation.  Furthermore, the study shows that cardiac auscultation sounds can be accurately classified at a point-of-care level even in the presence of substantial distortions.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance over matter only becomes prominent when the universe 
age reaches a certain quintessence-driven period, explaining the cosmic coincidence phenomenon. 
Furthermore, this theory predicts the universe will undergo a transition to a phase where both 
general relativity and quintessence are no longer governing laws, setting a time limit for our 
observational capabilities.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems remains limited in the context of computer science. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a sample dataset and conducted experiments to evaluate its performance. The study also explores opportunities for further development and offers panel design and scheduling algorithms applicable to general use cases.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and offer actionable advice to adjust experimental conditions for achieving optimal results. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks are created in different quantities from their antiparticles. To make this process possible, we consider several conditions including the requirement that one leptoquark be highly massive while the other remains light. To thoroughly assess this phenomenon, we examine various combinations of quark and lepton flavors to account for their possible interactions. To place concrete limits on this scenario, we apply theoretical constraints to experimentally measured values from the ATLAS and CMS assemblies of the LHC. By considering potential improvements to detection methods, our study provides guidelines for adjusting experiment conditions to maximize results. To provide context, we outline the historical development of this area of study from 1990 to the present day.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. A hidden Markov model and relevance learning technique allow it to handle time-dependent data, prioritize predictive feature dimensions, and prune irrelevant dimensions that introduce noise. As a result, our system excels in efficient learning for temporal sequences. Compared to conventional techniques, incorporating simultaneous supervised learning and metric adaptation enhances prediction accuracy by up to 25% and improves model interpretability through visual temporal sequence analysis.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier than $1\,\mathrm{TeV}$, their presence would conflict with constraints from electroweak precision data and the Higgs boson properties. We also find it challenging to reconcile the discrepancies without inducing sizable contributions from the anomalous interactions to the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing and the electron and muon masses. Nevertheless, the model offers a viable framework for the anomalies, and it can be probed by high-precision experiments in various processes, including $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ and $B^0$-$\overline{B^0}$ mesonology, as well as deep-inelastic scattering and LEP.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set is
sampled multiple times, with each sample being affected by some error.
The goal is to determine the original sequence before the errors occurred.
It is capable of modeling various real-world situations such as genetic sequence
reconstruction, data transmission, and disk storage error recovery.
The focus of this research on the sequence reconstruction problem is on
permutations with the Hamming distance, using a particular error model.
It aims to find an error-bound estimate that would provide insight into the
sequences that can be accurately reconstructed.
Three distinct approaches to solving the sequence reconstruction problem are
proposed: dynamic programming, a linear program-based method, and a bicriteria
approxiimation algorithm.
It is demonstrated that the first approach yields optimal solutions for certain
problem variants, while the second approach offers another solution that can be
useful in specific scenarios.
The third approach, using a bicriteria approximation algorithm, is capable of
providing near-optimal solutions for certain problem sizes.
It is also shown that an error-bound estimate of the Hamming distance of $2r-1$
can be attained using a bicriteria approximation algorithm with a Hamming distance
of $4k$ for a specific error model.
The main advantage of this error-bound estimate is that it is closer to the
Guarantaed Hamming distance of $2r

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners.
