We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. Nevertheless, we find that the accuracy of these analytic expressions is sufficient for modeling PTA parameters, but we do identify a specific scenario in which a slight discrepancy arises. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even narrow binaries with low masses below their merger rate can be within the sensitivity of future PTA experiments under certain conditions.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A clear, concise explanation is provided for each model section, supplemented by numerical solutions and graphical illustrations where applicable. Although this survey focuses on SARS-CoV-2, the discussions on epidemic modeling, compartment analysis, and model extensions are relevant to modeling future epidemics.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. Our system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. To achieve this, we have derived an equivalent two-component model consisting of an overpopulated spin component and a single quantum unit of Bose-Einstein condensation in a mixture of two species that can coexist. We have also examined laser-induced three-body recombination, which can convert atoms into molecules. By applying a Markov process and calculating the rate of recombination per pair, we have simulated the atom-molecule conversion process. Furthermore, we have investigated the parameters that influence this conversion, including light scattering, pair annihilation, and beam intensity. Our findings highlight the potential for controlled atom-molecule conversion, and we show that in optimal conditions, the efficiency of this conversion can approach 50%. Our study is relevant to current experiments involving spinor atom-molecule conversion and may also contribute to the understanding of pair formation in Bose-Einstein condensates.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture each pair of 20 base sequences serves as a unique, address-like identifier for objects in the array. To compensate for the limited ability to directly compare 20 base sequences, a intermediate indexing layer was devised using truncated DMTs that allow for the storage of hierarchical relationships among objects defined by the same primer pair. Furthermore, a method was developed to execute batch revisions on DNA storage. For instance, replacing the version number in all objects at least 5 generations below a given node in the hierarchy can be achieved with just one write operation involving the rerevision of the target node's parent node. The index is then updated at the T4 index level to point to the revised child node. Although the speed of writing to DNA storage is highly inferior to that of conventional storage systems, our research demonstrates that the slow speed of reading from DNA storage can already support a resource-constrained, real-time data access pattern. The performance benefits of using the primer pair as the identification method for data objects include a decrease in indexing overhead by a factor of at least 5 when reading from DNA storage. The novel techniques we have developed also hold promise for making DNA storage more versatile and practical.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established techniques.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolutions in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate thorough exploration of the complex relationships between gradient masking and various network parameters. Ultimately, our research reveals intriguing correlations between gradient masking and network architecture, including the effects of convolutional layer depth and nonlinearity on the prevalence of mask-based security vulnerabilities.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation at ultra-high frequencies. Our research develops a novel Bianisotropic acoustic metagrating design utilizing a honeycomb structure and investigates its acoustic properties numerically and experimentally at 100 MHz. Combined 2D/3D photonic-lithography techniques allow for the precise fabrication of these complex structures. Our experimental results show significant shifts in both reflected and transmitted wave angles, confirming our theoretical predictions and allowing for localized acoustic manipulation in the MHF range.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles. Evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at non-trained Reynolds numbers. Analysis of the reconstructed fields with established turbulent characteristics indicates that both the primary and secondary branches of the energy spectrum exhibit similar levels of accuracy as the training data, with minor discrepancies only present at high wavenumbers. Additionally, assessments of the reconstructed fields using wall-normal velocity statistics, cumulative distribution functions, and vector plots revealed that they match the characteristics of actual turbulent flows.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to these challenges, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the wild, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on the normal form's dimensionless parameter, $ \sigma $. The value of $ \sigma $ is, in turn, influenced by the prey's movement speed and the distance between the two predators. Furthermore, the model is used to create a quantitative indicator for early warning signs of a large amplitude oscillation, which can indicate a future population shift.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer NUV$-r$ colors of a given galaxy. The analysis indicated that NUV$-r$ color generally discriminated between galaxies with and without bulges more effectively than other existing methods. Bulges were identified in 53\% of the galaxy sample, and the majority of low-mass star-forming galaxies had a bulge in 79\% of cases, whereas the proportion of bulge-hosting galaxies decreased to 34\% among the most massive star-forming galaxies. A notable turnover in the $M_\odot$-SFR relation was observed at $10^{10.5}M_\odot$. By comparing the central and outer NUV$-r$ colors with the star formation rate, a distinction was made between galaxies with and without bulges using their color versus SFR relation. A sharp decrease in the color versus SFR relation was found at the $10^{10.5}M_\odot$ turning point. Furthermore, an analysis of the SFR versus mass relation for galaxies without bulges revealed a steep slope of -0.44, in contrast to -0.10 for those with bulges,

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen firmware vulnerabilities. Our research aims to mitigate the drawbacks of such protocols by implementing a corresponding fence instruction that synchronizes memory access and prevents unwanted side effects, including data reordering and access to memory areas with uninitialized or downgraded content. The proposed fence instruction can be seamlessly integrated into the protocol's existing architecture, and through practical, fence-enabled protocol simulations using FPU and FMA instructions, we have observed significant performance improvements, specifically a $3.57\times$ throughput increase and $2.26\times$ application performance improvement, without any energy consumption consequences.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical description texts, this approach is shown to effectively identify key aspects of lung changes associated with ICU admission, as validated through multiple metrics. Furthermore, the proposed method is compared to alternative, more complex approaches using a well-defined evaluation protocol.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we evaluate and validate the effectiveness of two state-of-the-art approaches, allowing for the selection of the most competent model and incorporating its output with an ensemble strategy. By applying BNPS and incorporating the scores from the two selected models, SABRA achieves notable improvements in accuracy and a significant reduction in false positives, especially on the challenging LIOA-VRD benchmark.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. We've experimented with multiple training and prediction methods including cross-domain techniques, as well as introducing an efficient yet straightforward approach for frame selection. Our results showcase a $13.50\%$ improvement in average accuracy compared to the current state-of-the-art, the most significant betterment to date, and a $11.50\%$ improvement over the baseline model.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been effectively replicated on FPGAs, our approach uniquely captures the parallel processing capabilities of this technology. By utilizing a non-blocking strategy for memory access, we successfully mitigated the occurrence of deadlocks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the functioning of our CAM/APP by running a K-means clustering algorithm, showcasing a significant increase in performance over traditional methods.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage of development, representing a transitional phase from star-formation to quenching.

We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing all relevant lepton sector observations and constraints. The analysis with updated data and refined techniques significantly diverges from the earlier prediction, and as such, we cannot confirm the UTZ model's ability to produce small non-zero CP-violating phases or a specific range for the absolute value of the UTZ coefficient. Moreover, we cannot rule out the possibility that the UTZ flavour model is consistent with the observed flavour data, and as such, we cannot rule out the possibility that the UTZ flavour model is physically valid.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis. The model is trained via a negative-log-likelihood objective with code connection data treated as supervisory signals. The resulting model is capable of generating complex code, including entire C functions, according to evaluation results from multiple datasets. Furthermore, our model demonstrates improved code quality compared to both a baseline transformer model and a version that is trained with actual code examples.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no signs of core breakdown. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address these challenges, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general form of the AoI distribution and derive an explicit formula for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison of these results to previously published studies on M/G/1/1 and G/1/1 queues reveals the importance of considering both AoI and packet age for understanding the discrete-time status updating system.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same type of algebras and by identifying specific conditions for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research significantly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust protection is a consequence of the intricate relationship between quantum tunneling, Coulomb interactions and the specific electronic structure of silicon, making this exchange interaction peculiar to silicon and potentially exchange-error-resistant when integrated with silicon-based quantum computing systems.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully demonstrated the potential for graph neural networks to generalize to novel instances of a system by leveraging available examples. In doing so, we showed that, given sufficient data, the learned representation can efficiently predict future system states with minimal additional training. Furthermore, we established that these representations convey valuable information about the system's underlying structure. In turn, this enables us to retrieve past instances with similar dynamics and structure, even in large-scale systems with limited historical data available. In pilot studies, our findings were supported across multiple disciplines, including physics and epidemiology. In physics, we explored the nonlinear dynamics of coupled pendulums, while in epidemiology, we analyzed the spread of diseases in multiple jurisdictions. In both cases, our approach excel in predicting future system states, past instances with similar dynamics and structure, and generalizable models to unseen time steps and system sizes with only a small amount of data available.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

A particular type of multipartite entanglement known as unextendible product bases (UPBs) exhibits unique properties that can be used to measure the strength of quantum nonlocality in complex systems. In this study, we specifically focus on UPBs consisting of three or more systems and demonstrate the existence of strongly nonlocal points within these bases, even if the systems are not identical. In fact, we show that in systems involving more than two non-identical systems, the quantum nonlocality of these points cannot be described using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). To further explore the strength of this nonlocality, we developed a technique for converting UPBs in heterogeneous systems into entangled states of high quality, and found that this conversion achieves the highest fidelity when the systems involved are close in size. Additionally, we discovered that in systems consisting of two non-identical systems, the quantum nonlocality of UPBs cannot be described using LOCC, and found that in systems involving more than two equivalent systems, the quantum nonlocality of UPBs can be described using LOCC, with the caveat that this description may require an infinite number of applications of LOCC.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated under various conditions involving random target distributions and observations, showing improved convergence speed and cooperative stability in all scenarios. The code's responsiveness and stability are guaranteed by implementing numerical techniques such as artificial compression, stiff boundary treatment, and astrobot stability monitors. The experimental results confirm that our method can handle the complex coordination of astrobots in SDSS-V and converge to a stable state in a quarter of the time it takes for an uncoordinated, random placement of astrobots.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly. In contrast, recovering the exact orientation of cameras from EXIF data is not feasible due to the limited available information. Consequently, camera calibration becomes an unsolved problem in conventional panoramic stitching methods. In our work, we circumvent this challenge by leveraging the aforementioned assumption to reduce necessary camera calibration inputs. Specifically, we need only determine the relative orientation between pairs of cameras rather than undertaking a comprehensive calibration process. Leveraging OLS for efficient 3D point computation, we derive an updated 7-Point solution for relative orientation problems. Moreover, we introduce a novel approach to handle outliers resulting from noisy sensor data. In contrast to traditional RANSAC methods, our proposed solution yields substantially faster execution times. In addition to this new approach, we introduce an innovative way to manage the ordering of scans in a panoramic sequence. We experimentally evaluate our method against a diverse and extensive dataset consisting of 29 test scenes, obtaining notable enhancements in processing speed and accuracy compared to conventional methods like SIFT and SAM.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a basic two-fluid model that includes distinct vapour and air phases and models their interaction through exchange coefficients. Further, a simple single-column model incorporating this two-fluid approach is utilized to study Rayleigh-Benard convection, a fundamental phenomenon in nature where enclosed water is heated from below. Results from this experiment were compared to those from various other convection studies, demonstrating that the choice of solver has a significant impact on heat transfer coefficients. Ultimately, the findings from this study suggest that the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection may be achieved through the application of a multi-resolution single-column model.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions.
